## Fitting several curves

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: how could we fit this model, one spline per input?

Two minutes. Expected: one curve at a time, each fitted to what the others leave; the next slide is the answer.
:::

::: {.ask}
We know how to fit a spline to one input: least squares on its basis matrix. How could we fit a model with a curve for each of several inputs?
:::


## Backfitting algorithm

::: {.notes}
The legacy "Backfitting algorithm", rewritten. Iteration t updates the curves in turn, each from the latest fit of the others: the curves before j are already at iteration t, those after j still at t - 1. Centering keeps the constants from drifting between components, since only their sum is determined. Vectors: x_j is the column of input j, and f_k(x_k) applies f_k to each of its n entries.
:::

Model: $\hat f(\mathbf x) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat f_1(x_1) + \cdots + \hat f_p(x_p)$. Columns $\mathbf x_1, \ldots, \mathbf x_p$; $\hat f_k(\mathbf x_k)$ is the vector of fitted values of curve $k$

1. Initialize: $\hat\beta_0 = \bar y$, and $\hat f_j^{(0)} = 0$ for every $j$
2. For iteration $t = 1, 2, \ldots$:
    - for $j = 1, \ldots, p$:
        - partial residual $\mathbf r_j^{(t)} = \mathbf y - \hat\beta_0 - \sum_{k < j} \hat f_k^{(t)}(\mathbf x_k) - \sum_{k > j} \hat f_k^{(t-1)}(\mathbf x_k)$
        - $\hat f_j^{(t)}$: a one-input smoother (e.g. a spline) of $\mathbf r_j^{(t)}$ on $\mathbf x_j$, centered to mean zero
    - stop when iteration $t$ barely changes the fitted values

## Backfitting and partialling out {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Two centered inputs, so beta_0-hat = y-bar drops out. Each line of the display is one pass of the inner loop: the one-input least-squares slope of its partial residual, using the other slope's latest value; beta_2-hat^(0) = 0 is step 1. A fixed point satisfies both normal equations, so it is least squares. With standardized inputs of correlation rho, each iteration multiplies the distance to least squares by rho squared: the next slide shows what that looks like.
:::

Two centered inputs, and a line for each component: $\hat f_j(x) = \hat\beta_j x$. Start at $\hat\beta_2^{(0)} = 0$. Iteration $t$ fits each slope to its partial residual:
$$
\hat\beta_1^{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf x_1^T\big(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_2^{(t-1)} \mathbf x_2\big)}{\mathbf x_1^T \mathbf x_1}, \qquad
\hat\beta_2^{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf x_2^T\big(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_1^{(t)} \mathbf x_1\big)}{\mathbf x_2^T \mathbf x_2}
$$

. . .

The slopes stop changing only where both hold: $\mathbf x_j^T(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_1 \mathbf x_1 - \hat\beta_2 \mathbf x_2) = 0$ for $j = 1, 2$. These are the normal equations: the fixed point is least squares

::: {.retrieval}
Partialling-out theorem: the coefficient on $\mathbf x_2$ is $\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y / \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2$, the slope on what is left of $\mathbf x_2$ after $\mathbf x_1$ has explained what it can.
:::

Backfitting does this with smooth curves instead of lines

## Backfitting on the films



::: {.notes}
Smoothing splines with 8 effective parameters each (smooth.spline, df = 8), not mgcv's penalties, so the curves differ a little from the last fit. Length and Short have correlation -0.65, so rho squared would suggest fast convergence; but the length curve can bend to mimic the Short flag, which a line cannot, so the iterations shrink the distance far more slowly. The coefficient is within 1% of its final value after 66 iterations.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](08-1-ensembles_files/figure-revealjs/backfit-films-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1650}
:::
:::


Length, year and Short on the training films, starting from zero. Length and Short are closely related: each iteration moves a little more of the shorts' higher ratings from the length curve to the Short coefficient, which settles after about 70 iterations

## Backfitting, more generally {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Skip if behind. Gauss-Seidel solves a linear system one unknown at a time, using the latest values; on a least-squares problem it is coordinate descent, and with a block of unknowns at a time, block coordinate descent. Gram-Schmidt is ESL's "regression by successive orthogonalization" (Algorithm 3.1). With a smoother that is not least squares, such as loess, backfitting and residual-on-residual give different estimates.
:::

**Any number of inputs.** With one coefficient per input, each update minimizes the RSS over that coefficient with the others held fixed: **coordinate descent** (Gauss–Seidel, in numerical linear algebra). A spline gives each input a block of coefficients, updated together: **block coordinate descent**. Fast for unrelated inputs, slow for strongly related ones

**Gram–Schmidt** residualizes each input (predictor) on the ones before it, once. Backfitting leaves the inputs alone and residualizes $\mathbf y$ iteratively

**Partialling out with flexible fits.** Residualize both $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf x_j$ on the other inputs, with any regression method, then regress residual on residual: **double machine learning**, later in the course

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: for an additive fit, each component curve is a partial dependence plot; when the truth has interactions, the additive model is importantly wrong.
:::

## Partial dependence plots for a GAM

::: {.notes}
The figure from "Replace each linear coefficient with 2d plot", again. For an additive fit the partial dependence of f-hat on x_j is f_j-hat plus a constant, so these are its partial dependence plots; the definition for any model is next lecture's.
:::

These univariate plots for GAMs are called **partial dependence plots** (PDPs). They show how the GAM depends on each feature: a simple one-dimensional dependence, because of the additivity assumption

But what if additivity is wrong?

## All models are wrong {minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
Box (1976), section 2.4, "Worrying selectively", checked against a scan of the paper; the regression lecture had it too. Box and Draper (1987), p. 74, as Wikipedia and others cite it: the book was not checked. The link is the Wikipedia article on the aphorism. It sets up "importantly wrong" on the next slide. Photo: UW–Madison Archives, ca. 1974 (S11438), supplied by the convenor; the archive's rights statement was not checked.

[All models are wrong, but some are useful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_models_are_wrong)

> Since all models are wrong the scientist must be alert to what is **importantly wrong**. It is inappropriate to be concerned about mice when there are tigers abroad.

Box (1976)

> Remember that all models are wrong; the practical question is how wrong do they have to be to not be useful.

Box and Draper (1987)

## Can additivity/GAMs be *importantly wrong*?

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, the calculus half. The causality half comes after the interactions, briefly; later in the course a model's curve is compared with an effect.
:::

Interpretation: think carefully about **calculus** and **causality** (causality: briefly, after the interactions). To simplify let's consider the identity link function (rather than e.g. logistic regression, those cases are more complicated)

#### Calculus

Does the CEF really decompose into additive terms?  Is this approximation good:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \mathbb E[Y | \mathbf X] \approx g(x_j)
$$
Or does the relationship between the average of $Y$ and $x_j$ vary depending on the value of another predictor $x_k$?

## Interactions in the movies data



::: {.notes}
Legacy "Interactions" and "Misspecification", merged. Decades, not years (too few films in one year), and non-shorts only (the shorts put a dip near an hour in every decade). The correlation of length with rating goes from 0.42 in the 1950s to 0.2 in the 2000s: a raw correlation, not a fitted interaction.
:::

If the slope in length changes with year, the derivative of $\mathbb E[\text{rating} \mid \text{length}, \text{year}]$ in length depends on year too, and an additive model is misspecified. Non-shorts, by decade:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](08-1-ensembles_files/figure-revealjs/movies-interaction-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1650}
:::
:::


## True model non-additive; GAM is wrong

::: {.notes}
Legacy slides from the interpretation deck, merged. The CEF (conditional expectation function, E[Y | X]) is x_1 squared times cos(pi x_2 / 2): a parabola in x_1 opening up where the cosine is positive and down where it is negative, which average to almost nothing. The legacy text wrote cos(x_2).
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f1 <- function(x) x^2
f2 <- function(x) cos(pi * x / 2)
df_int <- tibble(x1 = runif(2000, -1, 1), x2 = runif(2000, -4, 4)) |>
  mutate(y = f1(x1) * f2(x2) + rnorm(2000))
fit_gam_wrong <- gam(y ~ s(x1) + s(x2), data = df_int)
```
:::


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](08-1-ensembles_files/figure-revealjs/int-gam-1.png){width=1110}
:::
:::

:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
The fitted component for $x_1$ is nearly flat: a parabola opening upward when $\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0$ and downward when $\cos(\pi x_2/2) < 0$ cancel when averaged over $x_2$

Additivity assumption is now (importantly) wrong
:::
:::

## Causality: what are we "controlling for"? {minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
Context for the next slide. The quotation is from the syllabus of the opinion (608 U.S. 85, at 88). Morris (2026) calls the rule "conditioning on a mediator variable"; the dissent made a related point. After the decision, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Florida moved to redraw congressional maps before the midterms (press reports, May 2026).
:::

*Louisiana v. Callais*, US Supreme Court, 29 April 2026, 6 to 3: evidence of racially polarized voting must come from "an analysis that controls for party affiliation"

- The majority's reasoning: the divide may be partisan rather than racial, so race counts only where it survives holding party fixed
- Critics argue that this misuses statistics: party is partly a **consequence** of race, so holding it fixed removes part of what is to be measured (Morris 2026)
- After the decision, several Southern states redrew their congressional maps before the November 2026 midterm elections

What would a GAM of vote share on race and party show?

## Causality: what partial dependence holds fixed {minutes="3"}



::: {.notes}
Simulated counties, not data: % Black from a beta distribution; party (% Democratic identifiers) rises steeply with % Black and then levels off; vote share is an S-shaped function of party plus a smaller direct curve in % Black. So the CEF of vote share given both is additive, and the GAM recovers it. Its partial dependence plots, on the vote-share scale: strong in party, much flatter in % Black (10 points over the range, against 88 without party in the model, the dashed curve, which comes after the pause). They show the direct paths only; race acts on vote share mostly through party. Which diagram fits, and whether the law asks about the total or the direct dependence, are not statistical questions. Next lecture: partial dependence for any model.

## Recap: the causal example {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: say the sentence. The adjustment theorem's condition, from the causality lecture: the mediator is a consequence of the treatment, so adjusting for it answers a different question.
:::

The GAM fits correctly, the plot interprets the GAM correctly, but the plot answers the wrong (uninteresting) causal question

### Part 3: building a tree

## The Star Wars films



::: {.notes}
The whole data set for the next few slides: the five Star Wars films in the data (Episode III came out after the data end), ratings as IMDb's users gave them up to 2005. ## RSS for each possible split {.inverse}

## The grown tree



::: {.notes}
The tree the last two slides found. rpart agrees: grown with no stopping rule (minsplit 2, cp 0), it finds the same 4 leaves. Every leaf holds films of one rating, so the training RSS is 0.
:::

![](08-1-ensembles_files/figure-revealjs/star-wars-tree-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1650}
:::
:::


4 leaves, each holding films of one rating: a training RSS of 0. Grown until it cannot split, a tree memorizes its training data

## Growing a tree



::: {.notes}
Legacy "Complexity and overfitting" and "Growing and pruning", reworked. Grown out, rpart gives 2,670 leaves for 2,723 distinct (year, length) pairs: it cannot split films that share their inputs.
:::

- **Recursive**: split the data by the most discriminating single-variable question; then do the same inside each leaf, and so on
- **Greedy**: each split is the best *now*. A weak split that would enable a strong one below it can be missed, so stopping early is risky: grow a large tree, then prune (next slide)
- **When to stop**: a leaf too small to split (rpart's `minsplit`), or no split that improves the fit enough (`cp`)
- Grown until no leaf can split, a tree is like 1-nearest neighbors: on the training films, year and length alone give 2,670 leaves

::: {.retrieval}
$k$ nearest neighbors average the $k$ training points closest to $x_0$; a tree averages those in $x_0$'s leaf, a neighborhood chosen by subsets of features
:::

## Pruning {.inverse}



::: {.notes}
Compress: for each alpha the sub-tree with the least RSS + alpha x leaves; the sub-trees are nested, and alpha is tuned on held-out data.

The grown Star Wars tree: 4 leaves, RSS 0. Thresholds: the prequels' split saves 0.18 for its one extra leaf, the originals' 0.33, the root 4.18; rpart's cptable has the same numbers divided by the root RSS. Why nested: for one branch, each way of pruning it costs RSS + alpha x (its leaves), a line in alpha whose slope is its number of leaves; cutting the branch back to one leaf is the line with the smallest slope, so once it is the cheapest it stays the cheapest as alpha grows. A branch cut at some alpha stays cut at every larger alpha (Breiman et al. 1984, ties broken toward the smaller tree). For one alpha, the best sub-tree is a dynamic program from the leaves up: at each node, the cheaper of one leaf and the children's best; the whole sequence comes from cutting the weakest branch, again and again.
:::

For each $\alpha \geq 0$, the sub-tree minimizing $\text{RSS} + \alpha \times (\text{number of leaves})$. The Star Wars tree, as $\alpha$ increases from 0:


::: {.cell layout-align="center" dark='true'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](08-1-ensembles_files/figure-revealjs/sw-prune-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1800}
:::
:::


Sequence of trees; tuning knob $\alpha$ chosen by cross-validation or held-out data

## Choosing $\alpha$ on the films {.inverse}

Compress: training error falls with every leaf; tuning error picks the size.

In rpart the sequence is the cptable, cp a rescaled alpha; rpart's own cross-validation (xval, 10 folds by default) fills its xerror column. Here the tuning films instead. In bagging and forests the trees are usually not pruned at all: grown deep, and averaged.

## Trees and missing inputs



::: {.notes}
Missingness incorporated in attributes (MIA; Twala, Jones and Hand 2008): each split also chooses where the missing values go, or splits missing against observed; Josse et al. (2024) recommend it because it handles both uninformative and informative missingness. xgboost's default direction is this idea (Chen and Guestrin 2016). rpart's surrogates (Breiman et al. 1984) treat missingness as a nuisance. randomForest stops on missing inputs (impute first, e.g. na.roughfix).
:::

The films' `budget` is missing for 87%: a film with no budget cannot answer "budget < c?"

- **Missingness as information**: a split also chooses which side the films with no budget go to, like its cutoff, to lower the RSS (xgboost's *default direction*); or a budget missing indicator that the tree can split on
- **Missingness as a nuisance**: rpart's *surrogate splits*, backup questions on other inputs that send the training films the same way; a film missing the split's input follows the best backup it can answer
- Informative here: budgets were recorded mostly for widely rated films (median 1,238 votes, against 71). Useful for prediction

## Part 4: three model improvement strategies {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: three ways to use many trees: average resampled trees, average trees that see random subsets of predictors, or add small trees one at a time. Legacy slide; "at each split" for "when resampling", and the boosting block no longer says what the next model is fitted to: "Adding trees" asks.
:::

Sacrifice simplicity/interpretability for prediction accuracy

#### **Bagging**\*: bootstrap aggregating

- Resample training data, average resulting models

#### **Random forest**

- Randomly drop predictors at each split

#### **Boosting**\*

- Successively add simple models to improve the aggregate

\* Can be used with other models too, not just trees

## Bagging: bootstrap aggregating

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, whole. A bootstrap sample, once, with an example: from rows 1 to 5 a draw might be 2, 2, 4, 5, 1, so row 3 is left out and row 2 counts twice. Row 3 returns on the out-of-bag slide.
:::

**Problem**: a single tree model can have high variance (like many non-smooth or non-regularized models)

1. **Bootstrap**: for each $b = 1, \ldots, B$  resamples (with replacement) of the training data, fit $\hat f^b$ on bootstrap sample $b$

2. **Aggregate**: combine the $B$ models, using majority vote for classification or mean for regression

$$\hat f_\text{bag} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^b$$

("Smoothing" useful for high-variance models)

## Averaging $B$ trees {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: variance of an average of B trees: copies, independent, correlation rho?

Two minutes, written. Expected: tau^2 (no reduction), then tau^2 / B; the third is the next slide. Collect all three first.
:::

Average $B$ trees' predictions at one input $x$

::: {.ask}
What is the variance of their average if the $B$ trees are

- copies of the *same* tree, with variance $\tau^2$?
- independent, each with variance $\tau^2$?
- each with variance $\tau^2$, every pair with correlation $\rho$?
:::

## Recall: variance of a sum

::: {.notes}
The identity the proof uses. Every ordered pair i, j with j not i: n(n - 1) covariance terms, each distinct pair counted twice, since Cov(V_i, V_j) = Cov(V_j, V_i).
:::

For random variables $V_1, \ldots, V_n$ and constants $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, every variance plus every covariance:
$$
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i V_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\, \mathrm{Var}(V_i) + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \neq i} a_i a_j\, \mathrm{Cov}(V_i, V_j)}_{n(n-1) \text{ terms; } \binom{n}{2} \text{ distinct}}
$$

## Correlated-average variance {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
The lecture's proof: count the terms (the last slide, with n = B and every a_i = 1), state, divide by B squared and regroup. Check: rho = 1 gives tau^2, rho = 0 gives tau^2 / B. Given the sample the bootstrap trees are independent, so rho tau^2 is the part of one tree's variance that comes from the sample; more trees cannot remove it.
:::

With $n = B$ and every $a_i = 1$: $B$ terms $\tau^2$ and $B(B - 1)$ terms $\rho\tau^2$, $\;\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_{b} V_b\big) = B\tau^2 + B(B - 1)\rho\tau^2$

. . .

::: {.leave}
**Correlated-average variance.** $V_1, \ldots, V_B$, each with variance $\tau^2$, every pair with correlation $\rho$:
$$
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\frac1B \sum_{b=1}^B V_b\Big) = \rho\,\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\,\frac{\tau^2}{B}
$$
:::

**Proof**: divide by $B^2$ and regroup, $\frac{\tau^2}{B} + \frac{B - 1}{B}\rho\tau^2 = \rho\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\frac{\tau^2}{B}$. Bagging shrinks the second term; $\rho\tau^2$ stays, since bootstrap trees grown from one sample are alike

## Random forest: dropping predictors

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: B is already 300: which term is left, and how could we shrink it?

A minute. Expected: rho tau^2; make the trees less alike. Legacy edits: predictors redrawn at every split, not once per tree; "(typically)". randomForest's default for regression offers p/3 predictors, here 3 of the 9.
:::

::: {.ask}
$B$ is already 300. Which term of the correlated-average variance is left, and how could we make it smaller?
:::

. . .

**Problem**: aggregation does not increase information if the aggregates are highly correlated, e.g. averaging 1000 trees but each one uses the same small set of predictor variables

1. **Drop** predictors randomly, at every split

    e.g. each split chooses among a random $\sqrt{p}$ of the $p$ predictors

2. **Aggregate** models which are now (typically) less correlated, achieving greater variance reduction

## Out-of-bag predictions

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, with the films. Training MSE uses every tree, including those that had the film in their sample, so it is too low; out of bag, each film is predicted only by the trees that never saw it, close to the tuning score. Once used to choose mtry or the number of trees, it is a validation score, not a test.
:::

- Each bootstrap sample contains some subset of the training data

- Roughly $1/e \approx 0.37$ portion of the training samples will be left out of each bootstrap sample

- Can use these to estimate test error (e.g. instead of $K$-fold cross-validation)

Software implementations may do this automatically

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
| A forest on the films, 300 trees | MSE |
|---|---|
| training films, every tree | 1.19 |
| training films, out-of-bag trees only | 1.50 |
| tuning films | 1.49 |
| tuning films, predicting the training mean | 2.00 |
:::

## Adding trees

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: add one small tree to the current fit: what should it predict?

A minute. Expected: the residuals, y minus the current fit; some will say the worst-fit films. The answer follows the pause: the same move as backfitting, which fitted each curve to what the others left.
:::

A forest grows its trees separately and averages them. Now grow them one after another and add them up: after $b$ trees the fit is $\hat f^{(b)}$, the sum so far

::: {.ask}
We may add one small tree to $\hat f^{(b)}$. What should it predict?
:::

. . .

The residual from the existing fit: $y - \hat f^{(b)}(x)$

## Boosting: iterated fitting on residuals {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: fit models one after another, each a small step toward the residuals; gradient descent with a weak learner for the step.

Legacy slide, after the answer on the last one; the ESL link is the current address, and two parentheticals are dropped (assessment information; "maximum inner product", unbounded without a norm constraint). The tree is found greedily, so it approximates the closest small tree.
:::

**Idea**: train models sequentially, decreasing residuals by a small amount each time. Each model contributes something different

Can use "weak learners" (e.g. trees with one split, "stumps") to grow an ensemble model gradually fitting closer to the training data

. . .

#### Relationship with gradient descent

**Gradient descent**: small step in direction of negative gradient

**Boosting**: small step in direction of *weak learner closest to negative gradient*

Instead of computing gradients, we reduce the loss by taking a small step in the direction of a weak learner: a simple, low-cost model

Optional additional reading: [ESL](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/) Chapter 10

## Boosting as approximate gradient descent {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Derived. The derivative is an ordinary one: the training loss depends on a model only through its n fitted values, so it is a function of n numbers and its gradient is an n-vector. A tree fitted to the residuals is the small tree closest to that gradient in least squares, found greedily, and it is defined at every x, so the step reaches new films. Notation: f-hat^(b) is the sum after b iterations, t-hat_b the small tree added at iteration b. gamma is the learning rate; ISLR writes lambda, which this course keeps for the penalty.
:::

The training loss depends on a model only through its $n$ fitted values $\mathbf f = (f_1, \ldots, f_n)$, $f_i = f(x_i)$: a function of $n$ numbers
$$
L(\mathbf f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \tfrac12 (y_i - f_i)^2, \qquad -\frac{\partial L}{\partial f_i} = y_i - f_i
$$
The negative gradient is the residual vector

. . .

A gradient step, $\mathbf f^{(b)} = \mathbf f^{(b-1)} + \gamma\,(\mathbf y - \mathbf f^{(b-1)})$, changes only those $n$ values. Boosting trees fits a small tree to the residuals, the small tree closest to the negative gradient, and steps along it, with **learning rate** $\gamma$:
$$
\hat f^{(0)} = \bar y, \qquad \hat f^{(b)} = \hat f^{(b-1)} + \gamma\, \hat t_b, \qquad \hat t_b \text{ a small tree fitted to } y_i - \hat f^{(b-1)}(x_i)
$$

## Boosting in practice {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, the grid-tuning half cut; the learning rate is gamma, as on the last slide. More trees in a forest settle to an average; more iterations of boosting keep fitting the training data.
:::

#### More tuning parameters

Number of trees/steps $B$, complexity of each tree/model $d$, regularization/learning rate $\gamma$. **Warning**: can now overfit with large $B$ (unlike bagging/r.f.)

Software may choose them automatically. *No guarantee it's reasonable!*

#### Bagging and boosting

Bagging and forests start with large trees, which have high variance individually, and average them to lower the variance. Boosting starts with weak learners like tree stumps, which have high bias individually, and fits iteratively on residuals to lower the bias

## Iterations and learning rate

xgboost on the films, trees of depth 2, at two learning rates; training and tuning MSE after each number of iterations, up to 10,000. With gamma = 0.3 the tuning MSE is lowest near iteration 173 (1.499) and then climbs; with gamma = 0.03 near iteration 602 (1.500), and it rises only slowly after; that minimum is flat over hundreds of iterations, so its exact place depends on which iterations are checked. Training MSE at 10,000: 1.10 with gamma = 0.3, 1.30 with 0.03. The mean alone scores 2.003. First on the cut order.

## Tree depth and interactions {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: one split for x_1 x_2? how many for x_1 ... x_p?

Two minutes. One split on x_1 at any c: each side averages x_1 x_2 over x_2, whose mean is 0, so both leaves predict 0 and the split gains nothing; the same for x_2, so greedy splitting stops at the root. A split on x_1 and then on x_2 in each child gives the quadrant means, plus or minus 1/4. For x_1 ... x_p a leaf predicts 0 unless it restricts every input: depth p, 2^p - 1 splits, none of which helps on its own.
:::

::: {.ask}
Can a tree with one split fit $f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2$ well? Hint: assume the inputs are independent, both $\mathrm{Unif}[-1, 1]$

How many splits would we want for $f(x_1, \ldots, x_p) = x_1 \cdots x_p$?
:::

. . .

A stump asks one question, so a sum of stumps is a sum of one-input functions: an **additive** model. Depth $d$: interactions of up to $d$ inputs

A boosted model is additive in trees, not in the predictors

## We're in dangerous territory {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Skip if behind. Legacy slide; the link now goes to the book (References), not a blog.
:::

- Less interpretable methods/models
- Many tuning parameters
- Increasingly sophisticated software with many defaults and/or automatically optimized tuning parameters

. . .

But consider, [Alfred North Whitehead](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/41568) wrote (1911):

> It is a profoundly erroneous truism, repeated by all copy-books and by eminent people when they are making speeches, that we should cultivate the habit of thinking of what we are doing. The precise opposite is the case. **Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them**.

## Conclusion {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: an additive model fits one curve per input, each to what the others leave; a plot of one input works best for additive models and can mislead when the truth has interactions; trees ask greedy questions, forests average them, boosting adds them.
:::

#### Additive models

One curve per input, each fitted to what the others leave: partialling out, one input at a time

#### Additivity vs interactions

A plot of one input at a time works most naturally for additive models, and can be importantly wrong when the truth has interactions

#### Trees and ensembles

Greedy questions, pruned by validation. Bagging and forests average trees to lower variance; boosting adds small trees, gradient descent on the fitted values
